items.title: Communicative Decision-Making in AI Chatbots: From Explicit Advice to Implicit Guidance
items.abstract: This study examines how two artificial intelligence (AI) chatbot systems respond to personal and emotional decision dilemmas, distinguishing explicit recommendation (direct guidance) from implicit influence (indirect structuring of the decision). Eleven standardized first-person vignettes were used, nine on romantic relationships and emotional decisions and two on social belonging and exclusion. Each closed with a request for advice. They were given in Turkish to ChatGPT 5.2 Plus and Gemini 3 Pro between December 2025 and January 2026, on new accounts with memory and personalization disabled, one after another in a single conversation per system. The 22 responses were analyzed descriptively and comparatively through qualitative content analysis, using a seven-dimension coding scheme covering normative framing, relation to uncertainty, emotional validation, decision ownership, presentation of alternatives, language tone, and level of recommendation. ChatGPT tolerated ambiguity, validated the user’s feelings unconditionally, presented options as an open set without ranking them, and left the decision with the user. It gave no explicit recommendation, but seven of its responses favored one option implicitly through maxims and conditional criteria. Gemini reduced uncertainty through structured, often hierarchical alternatives and evaluative framing, gave explicit recommendations in five responses and implicit ones in five, and drew on earlier turns of the conversation in every response after the first. These differences are textual features of two specific system versions; effects on users were not measured. The study describes how explicit and implicit guidance is constructed in chatbot responses and shows that a response without directives is not necessarily neutral.

items.title: Conceptual foundations of design and technological interfaces
items.abstract: This chapter examines the technological interface from a sociotechnical and interdisciplinary perspective.It describes the shift from the functionalist paradigm, which valued products by algorithmic performance, electronic stability and compliance with technical requirements, towards user-centred design, which holds that interactive systems must adapt to people's needs, cognitive limitations and contexts of use.Within this framework, usability and aesthetics are presented not as ornamental or independent attributes but as dimensions to be integrated.The chapter treats hardware and software as a single sociotechnical system: hardware provides the material canvas in which aesthetics first appears, while software shapes the interactive dynamics in which usability is experienced.The graphical user interface (GUI) is therefore addressed as the core of interaction, the space where functional and visual attributes converge.The approach is a conceptual, descriptive-analytical review of human-computer interaction literature, covering event-driven programming and GUI components such as icons, windows, pointing devices, menus and buttons, together with a brief historical account from Xerox PARC to the Macintosh and touchscreen devices.Drawing on this literature, the chapter states that interfaces based on visual metaphors and icons reduce the learning curve and cognitive load, and that an imbalance between hardware and software quickly undermines both aesthetics and actual usability.It concludes that a holistic, interactive approach grounded in user needs is required for products to be competitive, with user-centred design proposed as the framework for integrating usability and aesthetics in organizational settings.

items.title: Converting AI adoption capacity into institutional governability in higher education
items.abstract: Higher-education institutions can possess data, infrastructure, expertise, managerial attention and implementation resources sufficient to adopt artificial intelligence while remaining unable to direct, constrain, monitor, review and account for AI use as an institution. This integrative theory-building review proposes an explanation of that conversion problem by synthesizing organizational AI-readiness research, organizational readiness for change, responsible-AI governance, higher-education AI policy, and digital-transformation literature. AI-adoption capacity is distinguished from institutional governability: the former concerns resources and capabilities for credible adoption, whereas the latter concerns the capacity of an authorised institutional coalition to direct, constrain, monitor and revise a specified AI use. Organizational Readiness for Change is used as the principal explanatory lens. The synthesis proposes that conversion depends on governance change acquiring sufficient value, shared commitment and shared efficacy among actors whose cooperation is required; these collective states must be supported by workable authority, responsibility and resources. Evidence of governability becomes inspectable, for the AI uses that records capture, when authorized arrangements are enacted, generate traceable evidence, and are revised through monitoring and review. Higher education intensifies the problem because AI adoption can originate locally while obligations concerning privacy, assessment, research integrity, procurement, equity and accountability remain institution-wide. The resulting mechanism is not a maturity model, readiness scale or validated causal sequence. It instead identifies theoretically grounded failure points and a research agenda for studying why technically capable institutions may display fragmented AI governance.

items.title: Critical AI engagement framework: reconceptualising AI literacy as a structural and epistemic practice
items.abstract: Generative AI is now embedded throughout the research lifecycle, entering the formation of research questions, the analysis of data, the synthesis of literature, and the crafting of scholarly claims. Yet the dominant response treats AI literacy as an individual competency acquired through tools, skills, and frameworks. Even where competency frameworks recognise ethics, bias, or institutional context, these tend to be added as further attributes of the individual user. Critical accounts have begun to treat structure and power as objects of critique, but have not yet addressed researchers specifically: how delegating judgement to AI shapes the formation of knowledge claims, and through what relations researchers remain answerable for them. Building on this critical turn, we ask how critical AI literacy for researchers might be reconceptualised to address these questions. Drawing on critical pedagogy, decolonial thinking, academic literacies, and Ubuntu-informed relationality, we develop the Critical AI Engagement Framework (CAIEF) for researchers, repositioning AI literacy as a structurally situated and epistemically accountable practice, and apply it to research, and equally relevant to teaching. CAIEF is organised around three dimensions: structural consciousness, epistemic posture, and epistemic accompaniment. Together these shape epistemic agency, are connected through critical praxis, and map positions researchers move between rather than developmental stages. Epistemic accompaniment is the practice in which a claim passes through a relation capable of holding the researcher answerable, because the other party is also exposed to being wrong and answerable in turn. Generative AI reproduces the form of that relation without its reciprocal vulnerability, so epistemic work may be delegated while accountability cannot. We distinguish cognitive offloading, the delegation of effort, from epistemic offloading, where the delegated work forms, interprets, or justifies a knowledge claim, and illustrate how CAIEF applies across the research lifecycle. CAIEF thus reframes research integrity as a question of the relations through which researchers remain answerable for what becomes knowledge.

items.title: Democratizing Cognitive Capital: Public AI Infrastructure, Anti-Rent Governance, and Inclusive Growth
items.abstract: Productivity gains from artificial intelligence do not automatically raise worker or small-business earnings. Administrative labor-market records show rapid chatbot adoption and workplace task reorganization alongside flat average wages — a pattern consistent with non-pecuniary job amenities, workflow adjustments, and weak user bargaining power inside closed digital ecosystems. Extending the capital-concentration debate from physical wealth to cognitive capital — external compute, models, structured context, interfaces, and access rules — this paper develops an institutional framework for municipal public AI infrastructure. Rather than relying solely on ex-post tax transfers or grant-allocated research supercomputers, we propose a neighborhood utility hosted in existing public libraries and civic buildings: the Public AI Library Network (PALN), paired with encrypted, user-owned Personal Cognitive Cells. Using a Nash bargaining model with switching costs, we prove that platform-specific AI upgrades erode a user's output share unless external public and open options expand at least proportionally to platform surplus. We construct a four-stage Index of Public Cognitive Availability (IPCA), governed by multi-operator yardstick competition, sortition-backed civic councils, allowed-cost tariffs, and parametric public-private financing. Market cost estimates for a city of 13 million residents (450 branches, 11,440 accelerators, and 900 mentors) place annual cost at $5.1 to $7.3 per resident under 5-year hardware depreciation ($67 to $94 per active user at one million active users, vs. $1,200 to $1,500 annually for high-capacity commercial agentic plans). For deep automation regimes, we specify a rule-based citizen Automated Capital Investment Fund.
